In the context of multi-agent learning, our research focuses on developing a particle filtering-based framework, called EMPE, that enables robots to exhibit reliable social behavior.  By incorporating EMPE within our design, our robot is capable of effectively detecting and responding to its human partner's actions.  Through analysis of both human and robotic observations, our investigation reveals that EMPE exhibits the following key aspects:  (i) through inference, our robot accurately identifies and interprets its human partner's behavior, (ii) in response to these behaviors, our robot's action predictions become more precise, (iii) these action predictions serve as an intrinsic motivation for empowering its decision-making, leading to (iv) through these predictions, our robot's decision-making is empowered with Intrinsic Motivation, resulting in improved policies that enable it to accurately anticipate and align its human partner's actions, even demonstrating agency in a joint turning task.

We introduce an innovative paradigm for developing highly accurate and robust spectral analyzers across various settings, including extreme environments and locations. Our focus is on creating a universal model that can identify substances regardless of their composition, conditions, and locations. This goal is fiercely contested by existing methods relying heavily on data from the same domain. In contrast, our approach leverages contrastive learning to overcome domain limitations and our experimental results confidently validate our strategy. Our model, based on physics-based simulation, achieves remarkable one-shot generalization, surpassing current state-of-the-art models in accuracy on a range of challenging spectral tasks.

Two equivalent definitions of Lie 2-algebras are examined, along with their
corresponding linear versions known as Lie 2-algebras without a 2-algebra structure.
The survey reveals some recurring themes and challenges arising from these two
definitions, attempts to provide extensive relevant examples and offers a few
openly acknowledged unsolved problems. The majority of the work focuses on
(2,1)-algebras defined by two multilinear operators of degree 2 and 1, as this
definition is seen as the most natural and versatile.

Our research proposes LoFTR, a novel vision alignment method that employs only
pose estimation without relying on explicit feature detection. By treating image
registration as a masked self-attention task, LoFTR leverages the strengths of the
Transformer model to facilitate local matching across images. Since it doesn't
require detecting distinct features, LoFTR excels at cross-domain, cross-season,
and real-world challenges involving significant changes in appearance. On the NTIRE
2019 challenge dataset, LoFTR surpasses the state-of-the-art with a PSNR of 34.83,
an improvement of 1.28 points over the previous best method. The code for LoFTR is
available at https://github.com/acme-ai/loftr.

This study addresses the issue of mitigating bias in magnetic field measurements derived from the Local Correlation Fluctuations (LCF) method. Bias in these measurements results from a mismatch between the test-field orientation and the actual magnetic field geometry. To clarify, we have established that magnetic field structures with varying field orientations will introduce biased measurements, thereby compromising the accuracy of solar chromosphere magnetic field mappings. To address this challenge, we have developed two main strategies. Firstly, we have devised a method for identifying biased measurements. Secondly, we have proposed a technique for correcting them by incorporating two relevant constraints. Specifically, we have utilized the minimum energy method with two modified constraints to mitigate bias. In this revised approach, we have integrated an angle constraint aimed at addressing biased angles and a second constraint aimed at preserving mean intensity of the line. As our analysis of simulated data suggests, we have achieved substantial improvements in magnetic field structure precision. To validate these findings, we have applied our new approach to actual data sets and observed that the derived magnetic field configurations appear reasonable and in line with established solar physics principles.

Several studies have demonstrated the potential for Demand Side Control (DSC) to improve power network operating efficiency. However, past research has primarily focused on the costs incurred by power networks as a result of rising temperature, neglecting the energy consumption perspectives. This paper presents an independent DSC approach aimed at managing both thermal load reductions and energy consumption through a game theoretical method. This approach involves consumers strategically deciding on their behind-the-meter thermal load reductions and energy consumption actions. As a result, the DSC manager offers a price per unit of energy consumption as well as a price per unit of thermal load reduction, which serves to influence consumers to make informed choices regarding their actions. This method utilizes economic means to regulate consumption and encourages optimal use of air conditioning and other energy consuming appliances to minimize the impact on power network losses and distribution charges. Furthermore, we also examine the relationship between thermal load and energy consumption, which reveals that certain loads have a direct correlation with energy consumption due to reliance on energy-intensive appliances such as water pumps, which must be charged based on energy consumption rather than thermal load reduction.

A more accurate description of gravity is offered by Rastall theory which modifies general relativity by introducing an additional divergence-free energy flow term. This formulation has the advantage of making the gravitational field equations inside a spherically symmetric static black hole's interior diverge more slowly and ultimately allowing for a minimum radius limit to be imposed on singularity prevention, similar to the findings in general relativity. Here, we investigate the impact of Rastall theory's modifications on Hawking radiation from charged black strings. By taking into account both the impact of Rastall theory and quantum corrections on the vacuum state of a scalar field in these black strings for an arbitrary value of the Rastall parameter, we derive an approximate expression for the Hawking temperature. The impact of Rastall theory and quantum corrections on the black strings' temperature is thoroughly analyzed.

Let $T$ be a non-singular, conservative, standard ergodic transformation on a standard measure space $(X,\mathcal{B},\mu)$. This paper demonstrates that the spectral measure of a function $f$, which is part of $L^2(\mu)$ and satisfies $Lf = bf$, where $b$ is a continuous, real-valvalued function, is equivalent to the spectral measure of $Lf$. Additionally, we establish that the spectral measure of the iterated function $f^k$, which is also in $L^2(\mu)$ and satisfies $Lf = bf$, is equivalent to the spectral measure of $Lf$. This leads to the conclusion that $Lf$ and $Lf$ have comparable convergence speeds in ergodic theorems.

The research on very old and metal-poor stars within our Galaxy is crucial to understanding its initial metal content and chemical evolution. However, due to their low luminosity, these stars are difficult to detect unless they are relatively close to Earth. The development of new techniques aimed at selecting metal-poor stars using data from the Gaia satellite is essential for identifying such stars from among the vast number of observed stars. We present a new method for selecting extremely metal-poor stars, which utilizes the ratios of iron and alpha elements as indicators of the star's metallicity. This method relies on analyzing the BP/RP spectra available on Gaia, is insensitive to variations in the stars' temperature, and relies solely on the star's luminosity and metallicity. The method is calibrated using synthetic spectra generated from the PHESLM model, matched to the spectra available on Gaia, and then applied to the MMT/HIRPQ sample of very metal-poor stars. The sample's iron content was determined using the exact values from the spectrum analysis, and it is now possible to use the star's BP/RP spectra to estimate its iron content with a margin of error of 0.3.

The 2020 worldwide fire season ranks as the most severe of the century, largely due to devastating burns in Australia, Africa, and the US West Coast. Despite the scale of the crisis, the underlying causes and potential future trends remain poorly understood. To address this knowledge gap, we analyzed 20 years of global fire data from NASA's FIRMS system, using geographic information systems. Our investigation found that the 2020 fire season was the 10% most severe on record for each continent and that Africa experienced the highest percentage of severe seasons. Our analysis revealed several factors that contribute to a region's high fire potential, including urban influence, agricultural land use, historical burning patterns, and proximity to roads. By applying our model to a base map of the world, we predicted that 20-39% of the continents and 11-39% of the countries will experience severe fire seasons in the future. Our algorithm can be modified for other applications and our results provide valuable insights for predicting and preparing for future fires.

This study focuses on understanding lexical complexity, which is key to creating authentic materials for language learners. It investigates whether there are measurable characteristics that can serve as indicators of complexity in words. A database consisting of 20 languages, each with a sample of 1000 words, was used to analyze the relationship between the lengths of words, syllables, root words, and plural forms. A correlation metric, called McGert, was used to measure the consistency of these length indicators across languages. Through spatial data analysis, the study reveals a positive relationship between some of these complexity indicators. However, the strength and significance of this correlation vary significantly between different pairs of indicators. It was observed that McGert is most substantial for pairs of indicators that include word length. The study's findings have implications for the selection of complexity indicators in specific languages.

Our findings suggest that self-interacting dark matter plays a significant role in early-type galaxy clusters, particularly in altering the gravitational magnification of nearby galaxies' light in the context of weak lensing. By utilizing N-body simulations to model strong gravitational lensing, we discovered that a non-zero self-interaction in the dark matter field leads to a more uniform distribution of mass within halos, which in turn causes weaker gravitational fields at the galaxy's center. This is associated with a self-interaction cross-section of approximately $cm^2/cm^3$, which corresponds to a self-interaction cross-section of approximately $cm^2/cm^3$ at the $80\%$ confidence level. This is consistent with previous findings from research on the velocity functions of subhalos, which support a self-interaction cross-section of approximately $cm^2/cm^3$.

Model compression, a technique for compacting machine learning models, is highly effective at speeding up computations and reducing memory usage. However, it faces a significant challenge when it's impossible to obtain a model's full architecture or configuration. In such situations, standard compression methods that work well with fully accessible models fail to produce optimal results. The present paper addresses this problem by introducing a novel approach to model compression that works even when certain details are missing. It frames compression as a game involving player agents, where each player has the ability to alter either the model's architecture or its parameters. By taking into account the potential actions of all player agents, the method develops an optimized model architecture that allows it to resist unwanted parameters that might be induced by lack of access to certain model details. It's been tested on a variety of machine learning tasks, including neural ODEs, Mixture of Experts models, and neural Turing machines, with the results showing its effectiveness under a variety of scenarios.

This research develops a novel independent component analysis (ICA) technique called MK-Rapid ICA, capable of learning an inverse matrix (W)-called a de-mixing matrix-that accurately distinguishes non-linearly independent signal components by minimizing the covariance between them. By exploring the algebraic properties of matrix W's eigenvalues and vectors, called E-Normal Vectors and corresponding E-Normal Values, our method identifies those non-normality measurements known as abnormal scores that lie outside of standard normal distributions. By removing data features with abnormal scores, our technique identifies a subset of normal scores in a lower dimensional space and generates an optimal W-matrix. Experimental results demonstrating MK-Rapid ICA's efficacy show its applicability to data sets that contain outliers, using simulated data. Furthermore, we introduce a classification framework, known as MK-Rapid Classification, to identify cancer types in microarray data, utilizing MK-Rapid ICA's output. Our method's performance is validated using two cancer data sets, where it successfully classifies and distinguishes the different cancer types.

The number of traffic incidents worldwide is staggering, resulting in substantial losses due to reduced mobility and increased emissions. In low-to-medium developed countries where mobile network infrastructure is limited, crowdsourced data from social media provides an invaluable resource for monitoring traffic incidents and avoiding them. This study proposes a novel algorithm using spatio-temporal data analysis to accurately detect incidents. By analyzing crowdsourced data from Google Maps, we developed an AI model that can identify and localize incidents in real-time. Our solution also optimizes mobile network resource allocation and enhances incident detection accuracy by filtering out users not present at the incident. Experimental results demonstrate that our algorithm successfully identifies incidents and accurately estimates their duration. With over 90\% accuracy, our algorithm correctly identifies the E80's incidents as they unfolded. Moreover, our algorithm correctly estimated the time and location of the first incident on the E80 with an average margin of error of 6 minutes and  1.8 km respectively.

We examine the solution $u$ of the elliptic problem $-\Delta u = \mu$ in $R^N$ with $u \in H^1(R^N)$, $u>0$, given that $\mu$ has compact support. Considering the case where $R^N$ is divided into two parts by a $C^{1, \alpha}$ surface $S$, and with a signed measure $\mu$ concentrated on $S$, we establish the continuous dependence of the problem's solution with respect to small changes in the surface's geometry. Furthermore, this investigation leads to the development of a new elliptic obstacle problem.

Using computational models based on the universal Markov chain, we discovered, analyzed and evaluated yttrium cobalt boron compounds in their solid crystalline form. Our search uncovered five cobalt rich compounds that were previously unknown but exhibit potential as magnets and could be formed at temperatures below 800 K, below which cobalt begins to decompose. Two of these compounds, specifically YCo$_{13}$ and YCo$_{20}$, were found to be stable under normal conditions and exhibit a Curie temperature of approximately 373 K, significantly higher than that of other similar materials. Furthermore, they exhibit significantly greater magnetization than other similar materials and are highly resistant to changes in temperature. Additionally, we found that YCo$_{20}$ exhibits magnetic properties and magnetization that are highly consistent, as well as a unique and complex magnetic structure that varies depending on the specific atomic position.

An effective solution to the problem of risk-averse bidding in real-time display advertising is proposed, taking into consideration the constraints of a predetermined budget. The proposed strategy dynamic variance reduction framework directly minimizes a risk-based cost function, thus circumventing the need for approximate variational inference methods. As a result, it can accurately estimate the optimal risk-based cost without compromising precision. In contrast, state-of-the-art approaches rely on approximations that can lead to significant deviations from the true optimal result. Furthermore, this framework allows for seamless integration of various risk-based cost functions as long as they are differentiable. Its performance is demonstrated through numerical experiments conducted on publicly available advertising datasets, showcasing superior outcomes compared to traditional risk-based bidding methods.

Non-classical behavior in quantum information processing often manifests as odd Schrödinger cat states and quantum entanglement, which are inherently linked to each other. Recent studies have provided lower bounds on the amount of entanglement that can be generated through quantum steering, thereby indicating the relationship between entanglement and non-local steering. This paper examines the relationship between quantum steering and Wigner negativity, which is a localized resource, to conclude that Wigner negativity is not a sufficient indicator for quantum steering capability. Moreover, we investigate how local operations and classical communications (LOCC) can mitigate Wigner negativity and demonstrate that Wigner negativity can serve as a measure of quantum steering strength. The dependence of Wigner negativity on the quantum state dimension is also studied in the context of Wigner Negativity's resource theory.

Recently, an innovative idea of combining quantum key distribution with non-uniform random sources to amplify security has been introduced. This approach, known as RAIN, uses $m$ randomly selected states from $2^n$ ensemble $\rho_i$ to create a key, as opposed to a uniform random source. This method can offer significant improvements in practical scenarios, particularly when $m < 2^n$. However, determining the ultimate security of this scheme has proven to be a substantial challenge. A definitive security proof for RAIN has been demonstrated, which confirms that it can offer almost the same level of security as a traditional quantum key distribution using uniform random sources, albeit with slightly reduced efficiency. This security demonstration is based on two key concepts: the decoupling technique and a hybrid entanglement purification procedure. This proof is applicable to a variety of QBER regimes and real-world scenarios, which makes it highly valuable in practical applications.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in flat space, are always null curves, regardless of their direction. We then demonstrate that non-null Bertrand curves can indeed exist in four-dimensional pseudo-Euclidean space. An example is provided to illustrate this possibility. Furthermore, it is theoretically confirmed that Bertrand curves in flat space are always maximal. This finding leads to two key implications: (1) all non-maximal Bertrand curves in flat space are null curves, and (2) the Bertrand parameter 'p' is always constant for Bertrand curves in flat space.

The sampling distribution of the generalized Estimator $T_0$ for the scale parameter $\sigma_0^2$ in Feller diffusion remains largely unexplored. This research aims to shed light on this problem by demonstrating that the generalized Estimator $T_0$ is a sufficient statistic for combining information from two independent sample datasets. We will showcase the versatility of the Pitman kruskal-break ties rank order statistic estimator $T_{0D}$ and reveal its connections with the Tornqvist estimator. Through a weight function analysis, we will show the Tornqvist estimator to be the optimal solution in Feller diffusion. Simulation studies will be conducted to compare the performance of the rank order statistic, Tornkvist, Maximum Likelihood, and RMLE estimators.

In this work, we develop a new method to analyze the scattering of multi-photon states in waveguide QED systems using an innovative diagrammatic approach. Unlike traditional methods, our approach seamlessly handles an infinite number of internal degrees of freedom in the system's Hamiltonian, which describes the interaction between light and matter. By employing a specific parameterization, we are able to accurately diagrammatically represent the physical Hamiltonian and its equivalent in the scattering basis. This breakthrough enables us to systematically derive a systematic effective theory for multi-photon states in waveguide QED systems. Furthermore, we apply our approach to examine the scattering of two photons in systems consisting of multiple qubits, which leads to the derivation of consistent effective couplings between photons, thereby confirming the conservation of lattice symmetry.

A potential cosmological model with spin-dependent properties is presented in this research. The boosted dark energy component with spin is introduced to describe early universe phenomena such as reionization and cosmic diffusion. The model's equation of state, j factor, and spin-dependent diffusion equation have been derived. Additionally, parameters for the model have been estimated using supernovae data, magnetic monopole flux, large scale structure, and Hubble parameter data. Estimated boost velocity ranges from 0.0006c to 0.0009c and the spin-dependent EoS parameter, ω_ψ, varies between -1 and -0.99. The findings suggest that the spin-dependent boosted dark energy component might be insufficient to fully explain observed large scale structure data within the non-relativistic speed limit due to the inability of the model to accommodate a high enough j factor, even when considering a 5% fluctuation in the surface density of magnetic monopoles. However, when the model is constrained using supernovae, LSS, Hubble parameter, and radio survey data, it is able to yield reliable results. The research also demonstrates that the spin-dependent boosted dark energy component can successfully describe various cosmological phenomena, including reionization, cosmic diffusion, and the late-time acceleration of the universe. Furthermore, the model's predicted magnetohydrodynamic behavior and its effects on the late-time acceleration of the universe have been analyzed using time-evolving EoS parameters.

This note employs Bernoulli polynomials and their derivatives to illustrate and prove Faulhaber's Formula for the sum of the $n$th power of consecutive integers, along with a related generalization discovered by Stanislaw Ulam.

This research investigates how a method of signal matching called cyclic delay detection can be applied in detecting continuous-phase modulation (CPM) without coherence, revealing its underlying mathematical structure and thus explaining its increased complexity relative to matching filter-based methods, which shows that the former can incur significant additional complexity. The additional complexity arises from the need to perform multiple comparisons, which leads to an exponential increase in computational load as the number of possible delay values grows. The potential implementation of the detection method by means of a convolutional decoder appears promising, given its potential to leverage established infrastructure from existing receivers. The study further reveals that enhancing the delay detection criterion leads to a greater risk of incorrect detections, which in turn can greatly increase computational complexity, suggesting the importance of finding an optimal balance between these factors. The potential of using soft decision decoding appears particularly promising, given its capacity to exploit structure in the decision metric, which could lead to more efficient soft decision decoding techniques, which in turn could lead to more efficient decoding in delay detection, which in turn could lead to more efficient delay detection, which in turn could lead to more efficient receivers, which in turn could lead to more efficient cpm transmission, which in turn could lead to more efficient cpm networks, which in turn could lead to more efficient cpm systems, which in turn could lead to more efficient cpm channels, which in turn could lead to more efficient cpm links, which in turn could lead to more efficient cpm flows, which in turn could lead

Over recent years, reward learning, a field within AI research focused on creating intelligent agents through interaction-based techniques, has produced remarkable results. This study aims to enhance the efficiency of reward learning by combining two concepts: visually accessible state representations and cluster ranking. We propose a method, VACOR, where an image segmentation model is integrated with a reward learning algorithm to improve reward efficiency and optimality. VACOR's effectiveness was tested in a simulated environment, producing promising results and shedding light on potential future applications to reduce the time and effort required for reward learning. These findings are presented in a two-phase study, starting with a theoretical foundation that establishes the connection between visually accessible state representations and cluster ranking, and ending with a practical implementation and evaluation of our proposed VACOR framework.

On the premise that nucleons are composed of two quarks, our investigation of nucleon distribution functions is adapted from conventional space-time to noncommutative space-time, characterized by a specific commutator relationship. Unlike in conventional space-time, the noncommutative space-time reveals separate distribution functions for u- and d-quarks within the nucleon, which also displays an inverse relationship between the mass of these quarks and a specific noncommutative scale parameter. Additionally, our analysis shows that the noncommutative space-time influences the parton distribution functions at small x values, which aligns with recent findings from the HERA experiment.

In this investigation, a previously unexamined class of boundary-driven quantum circuits is introduced, which incorporates the Kitaev edge, a three-dimensional topological entity within a higher-dimensional quantum model. Specifically, this research enters this entity into variations of the Kitaev-Queensland code, a well-known 3D topological code, under the constraints of 2D lattice environments. Additionally, a detailed analysis is provided in relation to the quantum healing dynamics initiated by non-metric interactions in the quantum model.

We investigate large real-world matrices with disordered properties, and real-valued linear transformations that change certain row or column blocks of these matrices. Our analysis focuses on how a critical phase transition in the transformed matrices relates to a complex spin system on a rapidly connecting graph, with the transfer of disorder to the critical point facilitated by the transformations' structural constraints. 

Using the high temperature expansion of the spin model, with the matrices' eigenvalues treated as classical variables, we found that the behavior of the transformed matrices in the critical phase can be approximated as follows: For transformations with blocks of a particular size (the number of rows times the number of columns), the probability of certain extreme behavior decreases as the logarithm of the transformation's rank, for transformations with blocks of a different size (the number of rows times the number of columns), the probability of certain extreme behavior decreases as the square of the transformation's rank. 

Our approximation also allows us to estimate the distribution of certain parameters related to the critical point of the transformed matrices. Our method uses the Green's function and the high temperature expansion of the spin model, with the equivalent equations of the complex spin model treated as a variational problem.

Recent advances in pre-trained conversational models have significantly improved performance on various tasks within conversation understanding, though their reliance on large, randomly sampled dialogue datasets means their inductive biases are essentially neutral. This makes it uncertain what specific conversation understanding skills these models have learned, especially since many are based on task-specific fine-tuning without any theoretical foundation. To address this, we develop a meaning-tracking framework to pre-train conversational models in an unsupervised manner, incorporating meaning-tracking objectives to simulate human understanding of conversations through interpretation. This framework is built upon an existing model architecture, leveraging its ability to represent meanings through symbolic manipulation. We test our framework with three English conversational datasets, comparing its performance to models trained using standard random sampling and monolingual cutting-edge models. Results show our framework outperforms these models on various understanding tasks, and through thorough analysis of model behavior, we confirm its successful implementation of meaning-tracking for conversation understanding.

To develop a more comprehensive understanding of interpretability, we evaluated a novel learning algorithm, XOrLearning, designed to mimic how humans learn through successive examples of binary X-or-N values. XOrLearning's performance was evaluated in terms of its ability to learn and predict 2-bit values, as well as its capacity to adapt to varying scenarios, such as biased or unevenly distributed input values. To facilitate easier comparison with other algorithms, we created a simplified, text-based version of XOrLearning and refined its functionality with the addition of 'clarity metrics' to better understand its decision-making processes. Furthermore, we developed a standardized testing suite to ensure fairness and consistent standards of comparison. Our research also identified and analyzed specific errors made by XOrLearning in challenging scenarios, such as edge cases involving small and large values, in an effort to better its performance and develop strategies for remediation. Ultimately, this study provides valuable insights into the development of future machine learning algorithms, emphasizing the importance of transparency and straightforward behavior, particularly in situations involving complex or ambiguous input values.

Outlier identification is a crucial process in various Data Science initiatives. 
This research introduces TiWS-iForest, a novel method for detecting anomalies in data, 
combining the isolation tree algorithm with weakly-guided machine learning approaches. 
The proposed technique utilizes image isolation tree features, 
which are combined using bagging to increase the robustness and accuracy of anomaly detection. 
The method was tested and validated on the MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets. 
Results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, with the tiForest variant exhibiting a 5x speed increase compared to traditional methods. 
Additionally, tiWS-iForest retains the high outlier detection performance of isolation trees 
while achieving a 6x improvement in computational efficiency. 
This innovative method enables efficient anomaly detection in large datasets, 
marking a key contribution to the outlier detection field.

A novel approach to modeling extreme events uses transformations of minimal-length paths connecting discrete-time Poisson processes, which effectively encapsulates numerous extreme value models as special cases, including the use of prior distributions over parameter spaces to derive posterior distributions for modeling parameters. However, a significant shortcoming of this method is its inability to accurately model return periods, which are often utilized in practical applications. To address this limitation, we have developed a procedure that involves a direct transformation of discrete-time Poisson processes into return periods, which naturally arises from the use of thresholded observations. This new approach can also be viewed as a method for joint analysis of both partial and excesses above threshold values. Additionally, we have demonstrated that, unlike the original approach, this transformation yields both Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling results that exhibit strong, desirable dynamics and a natural separation between modeling parameters and quantities of interest, which significantly improves the efficiency of computational simulations by several orders of magnitude.

We analyze the scattering cross section in the optimal control framework, aiming to derive formulas for distribution and variance of cross section, and explore their implications. Our key discovery is that areas exhibiting stationary cross section values via optimal control method correspond to specific regular polygonal shapes, characterized by values of $cos(π/k)$ where $k$ is an integer. These areas also display an interesting property - their centroids lie on the hyperboloid $x^2 + y^2/z^2 = 1$. Focusing on the cross section distribution, we identify areas where the average cross section values correspond to specific geometric properties like the inradius, circumradius, and apothem of regular polygons. Similarly, the variance of cross section reveals areas corresponding to these same polygonal shapes with their distances from the centroid determined by the inradius, circumradius, or apothem.

This research focuses on a core aspect of natural language understanding - extracting common sense relations from text. It involves a large dataset, ATOMIC, which details causal, continuative, causal-instrumental, conditionally-progressive and resultant relations along with accompanying causal events. The project's objective is to design a system that can generate a logical expression or a numerical representation indicating the likelihood of these relationships occurring. The author proposed an integrated framework, COMET, which combines the precision of formal logic with the word embeddings and machine learning techniques of symbolic and neural systems, respectively. The framework consists of a dataset, ATOMIC 2020, which expands on the existing dataset by increasing its size (10 times), scope (4 new domains covered), format (annotated using multiple schemes) and type (annotated using both multi-part and binary response formats). The study demonstrates the superiority of its hybrid approach, which significantly outperforms both neural systems relying on deep learning and pure symbolic systems. Furthermore, the research demonstrates the utility of its framework by employing COMET to solve various natural language processing challenges.

We introduced a information reduction pipeline for the Hi-GAL survey, which translates IRAS and Herschel data into compatible formats. While Herschel data are already processed through the Hi-GAL Data Model (HDM), IRAS data need to be re-analyzed to be compatible. We employed the HIPE's native tools for the calibration and production of moment maps from both Herschel and IRAS data. Our pipeline notably generates compatible unified maps by selecting the closest large-scale galactic emission component to be subtracted from each region of interest. We validated the performance of our pipeline through the analysis of IRAS 61+40 and Herschel ring regions, as well as through the comparison of our results with independent maps obtained through independent analyses. Our pipeline's output, available at http://irasi.cfa.harvard.edu/, includes various integrated intensity maps, as well as maps representing total line widths and line-integrated fluxes, which are available through the Hi-GAL Data Release 2. These release include the results of two independent processes, as well as the comparison of Herschel and IRAS data.

The study of stellar composition and the formation history of globular clusters, particularly those in the Milky Way, can be complex and often presents conflicting results. Recent investigations using advanced techniques such as high-resolution spectroscopy have revealed varying initial metal levels within these clusters, although the evidence remains somewhat ambiguous. In an effort to further understand the formation history of globular clusters, we conducted new analyses of six NGC 2808 stars, focusing on the carbon and nitrogen compositions, which revealed abnormally high nitrogen levels and, consistently, low carbon levels. These results, achieved via intermediate-resolution spectroscopy using the HARPS-N spectrograph, confirm earlier findings of metal variability within this specific cluster, as well as confirm that the carbon levels in these NGC 2808 stars are indeed lower than average. The carbon levels were determined via the S ii/Ca ii and the O ii/Ca ii ratios, while the nitrogen levels were established with the N2/CaT and the [N/α] ratios. Notably, the calculated metal levels presented in this study are consistent at [Fe/H] = -1.51, -1.53, or -1.55, as the measured N2 and CaT indices, as well as the [N/α] and [N/F] levels, indicate a clear and distinct pattern. In addition to these findings, our data suggest a possible increase in the nitrogen levels within this specific cluster, as the nitrogen levels in these NGC 2808 stars are

A key component of understanding confinement effects is recognizing that exit times can provide valuable insights into the characteristics of the confining environment. In the context of a one-dimensional system, like a filament where particles move in a single-file arrangement, exit times can offer significant insights. However,, in more complex three-dimensional systems, the idea of defining an exit time is less straightforward due to the presence of multiple degrees of freedom. In the specific case of a three-dimensional system, where particles are confined within a filament-like environment, we have developed a method to measure the duration between entering and exiting this environment. Using our method, we have developed a theoretical framework for understanding the statistical properties of exit times in three-dimensional systems, including filament-like environments. We have found that the characteristics of the exit times in three-dimensional systems can be described by a similar formula as those observed in one-dimensional systems, indicating that the properties of the exit times are influenced primarily by the local confinement effects rather than the overall geometry of the environment. Furthermore, our results also show that the properties of the exit times can be described by a specific set of formulae that depend only on the local confinement effects, regardless of the overall geometry of the environment. In addition, we have also determined the speed at which the properties of the exit times change as the size of the environment changes. This understanding of the exit times in three-dimensional systems is expected to have significant implications for our understanding of the confinement effects in these systems.

Quantum Bayes' Theorem has been verified, confirming that proper application of the theorem yields consistent results in line with quantum physics principles. This finding validates the consistency of inferences made through the use of quantum conditional probabilities in the field. The frequently cited objections against Bayes' use in quantum physics by Mermin and Susskind have been specifically addressed, showing that the objections no longer apply when the correct formulation of the theorem is used in the context of quantum physics.

In high-energy quark-gluon plasma, QCD is characterized by a unique property called conformal symmetry, which results in a well-defined relationship between system size and temperature. However, as matter becomes more dense and forms hadrons, this conformal symmetry is broken, leading to complex interactions described by complex equations that depend on various correction factors. By applying established theories to the study of small quark-gluon plasma systems, researchers can deduce a fundamental relationship between the energy density and temperature, known as the equation of state. By deriving an simplified equation of state, known as the $\alpha$ parameter, researchers can gain valuable insights into the behavior of hot and dense matter across a range of sizes. This equation also has practical implications for particle accelerator experiments, as it can inform data-analytic approaches and reveal distinct QCD properties. By studying how this equation of state changes as it adapts to various scenarios, researchers can gain valuable insights into the matter's behavior across a range of conditions, from cooling to the emergence of conformal symmetry.

The Steenrod algebra's cohomology is generated by the mod 2 cohomology of compact Steenrod attractors, a discovery that was previously noted in reference \cite{KZ19}. Here, additional findings related to Steenrod attractors are presented along with an explanation of how they contribute nonzero, nonignorable elements to selected cohomology groups of the Steenrod algebra.

Astronomical research previously used the Lyman ultraviolet region of the electromagnetic spectrum to identify specific targets such as star clusters and star systems, but recent observations have revealed excessive contamination from Lyman-alpha foreground radiation, limiting the capabilities of optical instruments to operate in this spectrum range. Despite the existence of algorithms capable of removing Lyalpha contamination to some extent, researchers continue to face challenges of variable quality and unreliable results. A new approach, referred to as the Lyalpha Filter Model, has been developed to improve upon existing methods by employing a structured model of the Lyalpha foreground emission. This new model, paired with optimized parameters of the existing Roman RVS LSF, has demonstrated the ability to accurately remove the Lyalpha radiation, with results including the deconvolution and photometric reconstruction of the standard star Hipparcos 36, an M3 star, and the spectral deconvolution of the galaxy M81*1.

A new approach is developed to achieve coordinated subgroup control of large networks by using a decentralized communication structure. By leveraging graph signal processing techniques, specifically graph filters, a single centralized controller can directly translate desired actions for separate subgroups into individual control rules for network nodes, without needing detailed information about the network's structure. This framework ensures stable and consistent control signals for subgroups even in the presence of network topology changes. A numerical example demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach in real-world scenarios.

Our method of dynamic picture indexing enables the identification of consistently
appearing, localized features within sequentially received images, without the
need for image processing algorithms. This is accomplished through the use of
Kullback-Leibler divergence, which serves as a feature extractor and dynamically
assigns indices to these localized features as new images are received. The
current state of indexed features is represented by a vector, referred to as
the feature vector. These localized features may be interpreted as 'objects' within the image sequence, allowing their trajectories to be determined by comparing subsequent feature vectors. Furthermore, statistical analysis is used to identify correlations between 'objects' within the image sequence, with the goal of differentiating between synthetic and real trajectories, derived from random processes such as Gaussian or Poisson distributions. This research is an extension of previous work, specifically designed to evaluate the effectiveness of using indexed object trajectories as features within the applied dynamics of motion prediction and target tracking applications.

This study verifies the feasibility of a novel, unsupervised approach to error correction for binary linear codes within Gaussian noise. The developed algorithm, drawing on ideas from combinatorial optics and differential geometry, does not require initial transmission of encoded data, instead using received signals as its starting point to create a map between noisy space and a transformed version of noisy space, where each point corresponds to a code word with maximum likely accuracy. Notably, this unsupervised method exhibits performance comparable to the best possible performance for binary linear codes of limited size, slightly exceeding it for larger code sizes. When used for decoding binary linear codes of various sizes within Gaussian noise, this unsupervised method demonstrates results comparable to the best possible performance for low error rates and slightly exceeded it for higher error rates.

We examine the issue of uniform moveability within a class of periodic potential energies of the form U(x) = D(1 - ϕ(2px/N)) and identify the conditions necessary for it. The function ϕ serves as a comparison standard, and D and p are non-negative parameters that represent velocity and position, respectively. The study demonstrates that compared to non-uniform moveability in another class of energies (the Lissajous energies), uniform moveability is achieved with a broader set of D and p values when the comparison standard meets certain criteria, including an inner tangent circle and an asymptotic slope of at least one.

High-precision location and speed determination in 5G wireless networks relies on two critical processes - initial assessment and subsequent refinement. In the first stage, the network sends out a query and receives general location and speed information in response. The refinement stage involves the deployment of a network node, referred to as a remote unit, at the precise location of the target unit. Consequently, the target unit's response includes precise location and speed data. Consequently, the target unit's response includes detailed information on projections and the target unit's movement velocity. Nevertheless, the target unit's velocity remains unknown and known only by the target unit, whereas the network has only obtained approximate information. In this research paper, the target unit's velocity is referred to as the impulse velocity. This paper aims to develop Adaptable Local Projections (ALP), a novel localization technique that uses the received signal strength indicator (RSS) along with the received signal strength values, and the impulse velocity, to calculate the refined location and time of response calculation. In the case when the impulse velocity is unknown, this location calculation is also referred to as the blow-up location. ALP is based on an adaptable projection, which is derived using a generalized distance metric, generated based on a nonlinear distance function, and breaking down the search space into circular sectors. In each circular sector, the network deploys a linear based location estimate, and the received signal strength values, and the impulse velocity, to calculate the refined location and time of response calculation

A great deal of interest has been shown in the quantum version of the Casimir effect, characterized by the absence of virtual photons in the vacuum states surrounding a charged particle. This paper sets out to quantify this phenomenon by developing a mathematical framework for determining the angular momentum of the vacuum states surrounding a Landau charge. The research involves deriving an exact expression for the angular momentum of the vacuum states surrounding a Landau charge as seen through an observer in a rotating laboratory, utilizing the Fock space and propagator methods. The angular momentum of the vacuum states surrounding a Landau charge increases as the charge strengthens and the photon momentum increases, and this momentum can be up to 10,000 times that of the quantum version of the Faraday rotator, and the research offers a range of possibilities for the observation of the effects on the vacuum states surrounding the charge. The research offers a range of possibilities for the observation of the effects on the vacuum states surrounding the charge.

In recent years, bi-lateral attention models within the context of neutral word embedding have garnered significant interest, despite not being directly applicable to other tasks involving semantic representations. The majority of existing research focuses on developing new models for neutral word embedding, but this overlooks important applications in other areas. This paper presents a new framework, FGNET-RH, designed for structured text understanding and targeted at resolving challenges related to coarse-to-fine information, particularly named entity classification. The proposed framework leverages a fine-detailed KG to harness rich information and employs a refiner in hyperbolic space to minimize information loss resulting from mapping complex knowledge graphs to lower-dimensional spaces. The FGNET-RH framework comprises two primary components: 1) a dual attentional extractor that pinpoints and extracts detailed information from the knowledge graph, and 2) a refinement model operating in the hyperbolic space, which generates more precise entity classification results by combining information from the extractor and incorporating a soft mapping to allow for the incorporation of unrepresented entities in the knowledge graph. The proposed FGNET-RH framework offers a substantial improvement over existing approaches, as demonstrated through experimental results on various benchmark datasets.

This paper establishes specific expressions for the Hankel determinants of a particular type, related to starlike and univalent analytic functions, using established formulas and mean value results for the Laplace operator.

To address the issue of within-host contention caused by virtualization, multiple VP partitions are created inside each virtual machine, with each partition receiving a preassigned share of CPU resources. The number of VP partitions is determined by the desired level of contention isolation, with each partition configured to utilize a specific number of CPU cycles per second. This approach ensures that VP partitions are accurately allocated the designated number of CPU resources, while also preventing over-assignment to minimize performance overhead. The number of VP partitions is typically set high enough to ensure that at least one partition can provide the full CPU capacity without any constraints, allowing the host to run at its full capacity when not fully allocated.

In scenarios where multiple agents' actions are interdependent, finding an equilibrium point often proves challenging due to its computational intensity and non-linear nature. Building upon the Fixed Point Network (FPNet), which approximates the interdependence of agents' actions, we've developed the Equilibrium Networks (EQN), a family of neural networks that leverages FPNet to learn an equilibrium point. By applying the policy iteration algorithm with a differentiable representation of the payoff function, EQN can efficiently approximate the equilibrium by bypassing complex matrix calculations. We've demonstrated the effectiveness of EQN in training multiple agents to play various non-zero-sum, tabular games. Furthermore, EQN has the potential to be applied in various fields, such as reinforcement learning outside of the tabular context, by utilizing it as a basis for policy evaluation.

In decision theory, the concept of causal influence is crucial for determining how one random variable affects another, even after controlling for other factors. The focus is on developing a definition of partial identification limits for causal influence with applications in high-dimensional data. The definition uses a minimax optimization, incorporating all relevant variables to establish tight bounds on random variable causal influence. The definition is first applied to discrete variables and then generalized to continuous random variables, taking into account their probability density functions. The concept of high-dimensional causal influence is then examined, and methods to establish tight bounds on random variable causal influence are presented, including the use of convex optimization techniques. The definition and applications of partial identification limits in this context are a novel contribution, offering new insights into causal influence.

We develop an enhanced surveillance system for an LTI system being targeted by stealthy attacks. Using an offline model, our approach identifies unknown assault methods and establishes a predictive threshold for norm-bounded assault. It goes beyond current Bayesian solutions by framing the problem as a single statistical test rather than multiple comparisons. Additionally, we provide a confidence level for the test and expand our method to multi-assault cases. Our analysis connects our work to Stein's unbounded uniform confidence region, providing a foundation for effective surveillance under multiple assault scenarios.

A potentially effective solution to curb information overload is text summarization, although current systems are limited by their reliance on a small dataset representing only 5% of human languages. This research focuses on improving the performance of neural summarization systems for longer, more complex languages like Hindi, Tamil, and Gujarati, by converting them into more compact systems.
To address this challenge, we analyzed the performance of Graphical Abstract Machine, a monitored summarization tool, on an enlarged data set of translated English texts. Our study reveals that Graphical Abstract Machine produces high-quality summaries, surpassing the existing monitored systems. Furthermore, a newly developed monitoring component is proposed to enhance the system's ability to produce better summaries. Additionally, a large, annotated dataset was created to facilitate the development of unmonitored systems that match the performance of Graphical Abstract Machine.

We introduce the concept of S-rings of Noether type and demonstrate that they form a subcollection within the broader class of S-rings. Additionally, we detail the construction of examples in both finite and infinite dimensions, showcasing examples in both 3-dimensional space and higher dimensional spaces. These constructed S-rings will have properties analogous to those exhibited by rings of Noetherian type across different bases. Furthermore, in the case of 3-dimensional space, we prove that every subring which is correlated with these S-rings of Noether type will also possess properties analogous to those of subrings of Noetherian type. In relation to our previous findings, we leverage Hilbert's basis theorem to illustrate that in the context of finite dimensional spaces, every subring of Noetherian type possesses the capacity for ring isomorphism with a ring of Noetherian type. Consequently, this leads to the formation of a correlation between the set of subrings of Noetherian type and the set of subrings of Noetherian type across different bases, yielding a dimension-invariant property.

This research has obtained a comprehensive set of dynamic restrictions regarding the masses and locations of unseen celestial companions associated with five accelerated stars situated close to our own, namely AE Aur, AD Leo, AR Boo, AR Scor, and RX Boo. These companion details were deduced through the tested hypothesis that each companion's mass exerts a level of acceleration on its host star in accordance with the principles of Newton's law of gravity. While this hypothesis led to the identification of several potential companions whose existence is supported by current observational data, it is crucial to note that these results are sensitive to variations in the star's intrinsic properties, thereby highlighting the significant need for accurate star data. Building upon this foundation, future ground-based telescopes like the James Webb Space Telescope and the Giant Segmented Mirror KMT will be instrumental in obtaining this essential information, thereby taking a significant step towards potentially detecting the companion stars themselves.

Recently, researchers introduced the Square Variational Bayesian Autoencoder (SQ-VAE), a minimalistic generative model, and analyzed its expressive capabilities using existing theory. Although SQ-VAE exhibits superior performance in various benchmark tests, it suffers from an issue where it sometimes generates unrealistic data outside its training data range. This problem arises due to overfitting, caused by the model's tendency to fit the training data too closely. In an effort to overcome this limitation, we examine the conditions under which SQ-VAE can capture a precise, continuous probability distribution. When these conditions are not met, we propose the Regularized SQ-VAE (RSQ-VAE), which incorporates two regularization techniques to prevent the overfitting problem. RSQ-VAE's effectiveness is demonstrated through a combination of theoretical and practical analyses using a latent variable model, as well as through its application in multiple data sets from the Open Image Collection. These experiments reveal that RSQ-VAE not only produces more realistic images, but it also outperforms SQ-VAE in terms of both reconstructive ability and Poisson log-likelihood. RSQ-VAE's performance surpasses existing generative models, including VAE and VAEL.

A cutting-edge system has been proposed for integrating IoT in home security and surveillance systems through the application of blockchain technology and localization. This technology enables real-time monitoring of gadgets' movements in a home environment, utilizing GPS and GLONASS networks. The innovative approach involves utilizing a private blockchain to evaluate and validate smart tags' placement within a dynamic home setting. The flexibility of smart tags' design allows for diverse tag structures depending on the specific service required, which can include tagging individuals, belongings, or gadgets. When an object is tagged, a unique identification code is generated and recorded on the blockchain, effectively mapping a smart tag's location to a corresponding identification code. The dynamic nature of a home setting is accounted for through periodic adjustments in GPS and GLONASS signal synchronization, ensuring accurate and on real-time monitoring of tagged objects.

A widely used pre-computation method to speed up data processing is the gray coding technique, which uses error-correcting techniques to recover from transmission errors effectively. However, its accuracy depends on the proper estimation of L-values, a process that becomes impractical with large datasets due to the need for direct evaluation from the respective functions. To overcome this limitation, this research introduces an innovative approach that uses a deep learning model to predict L-values accurately and uses these predictions to reconstruct the original L-values for decoding processes. Our approach uses a combination of gradient optimization and reconstruction error to train the model, achieving significant L-value prediction improvement compared to baseline methods, and resulting in substantial rate-distortion gain for the binary codeword prediction problem. Our technique is adaptable to different function types and can effectively accelerate the encoding process using predicted L-values, but raises additional processing costs and reconstruction accuracy challenges that must be addressed. To mitigate these effects, our approach uses a threshold-based method to balance these costs and maintain a reasonable impact on the overall system processing time, ensuring that the benefits of L-value predictions are realized in practice. Our approach to predicting L-values and reconstructing codewords has the potential to significantly enhance the efficiency of the gray coding technique, making it suitable for various applications.

The objective is to develop algorithms whose performance relies on minimal parameters or single parameters with efficiently scalable complexities. The proposed techniques are applied to the problem of graph planarity in upward direction. Machine learning's prominent role in everyday life is a relatively recent occurrence, 
despite its century-long history which has largely gone unnoticed until now. A major 
barrier to wider recognition involves the complexities of gathering and labeling 
training datasets, particularly when considering the inaccuracies that can result 
from crowdsourcing due to the inherent uncertainty involved. Seeking to rectify 
this, our research develops a novel approach for tackling noisy, crowd-sourced 
training datasets that incorporate uncertainty information. A significant 
component of our method consists of an ensemble modeling technique which utilizes 
bootstrapped resampling to create multiple model iterations that can then be used 
to calculate the reliability of each model prediction within the ensemble. 
Additionally, our method incorporates the 'Human Softmax' distribution to model 
the uncertain output distributions of each model, thereby allowing for the 
calculation of a reliable ensemble output given an ensemble composed of models 
both accurate and inaccurate. Finally, our research utilizes entropic metrics of 
uncertainty in order to determine which models within the ensemble are most 
reliable. An application of this method to a well-documented dataset commonly 
employed in machine vision tasks, specifically the widely used MNIST dataset, 
confirms the efficacy of our approach in addressing noisy, crowd-sourced 
datasets incorporating entropic measures of uncertainty.

This research explores the norm behavior of the transfer operator for semiflows that stem from smooth, strictly expanding dynamics with invariant measures maintained through a finite-range or uniformly mixing interaction. Considering both conservative and dissipative dynamics, we find that invariant measures of the transfer operator exhibit exponential contraction, whose rate is tied to the spectral radius of a transfer operator's associated Markov operator. This results in the transfer operator's norm diminishing as, and decaying at a rate proportional to, the arctangent of a positive parameter related to the Markov operator's spectral radius. Consequently, we show that this leads to the transfer operator satisfying a condition related to rough regularity, and allows us to construct a version of the operator that is more closely related to the original, while maintaining preservation of invariant measures.

This research provides an exhaustive description of the parametric framework associated with minor strength-2 covering arrays. Specifically, it identifies the fundamental limits imposed by the covering array's dimensions, along with the minimum number of columns required. Moreover, it offers an algorithm for calculating the precise number of minor strength-2 covering arrays with a specified number of columns. Building on this framework, the problem of finding general covers for parameterized functions is defined, along with an algorithm that efficiently finds a general cover with a minimum number of columns for a given function. The method involves transforming the problem into an instance of the parametric framework and using its tools to determine the optimal solution. Additionally, the paper examines the efficiency of this algorithm and demonstrates its practical value by finding efficient covers for various benchmark functions. Finally, an assessment of the parametric framework's potential for broader application is presented, along with suggestions for further advancement.

In contrast to the certainty with perfectly connected statuses, uncertainty arises when individuals merely suspect the statuses of others, as a result, the degrees of optimality significantly fluctuate. This problem can be resolved through a computational method that involves converting a complex probability-based problem into a simpler one. This fundamental variation has led to the discovery that locally-known statuses can be determined as optimal through a computational approach. This finding holds true regardless of whether opposing actions are part of the strategy or rules that govern their use. Furthermore, this innovative result has enabled a broader implication - it now appears that optimal strategies can be definitively identified in various confidence-level scenarios.

In the field of software engineering, researchers often utilize the Windows Crash Repository as a wealth of data to explore ways to automate software crash replication. A prior study demonstrated the effectiveness of a genetic algorithm-based approach, but our current study seeks to validate this finding, keeping the problem-solving mechanism as simple as possible. By employing this method, our team was able to successfully replicate crashes on 87% of test cases, surpassing the 76% achievement of the prior study, with a notable 95% convergence rate, a marked improvement over the 30% rate of the prior study. It's crucial to note that our reproduction of this method made a concerted effort to maintain its original simplicity, in contrast to some potential improvements that could be explored in future research.

The arrangement of vortices within a superconductor subjected to an external magnetic field parallel to its planes is examined using a magnetically responsive, very high quality single crystal of YBa$_{2}$Cu$_{3}$O$_{7}$. At a sufficiently low temperature and magnetic field strength, a regular grid pattern of vortices emerges, characterized by square-shaped units with diagonal lines. As the temperature rises or the magnetic field strength increases, this square-grid structure transforms into another regular pattern, where the units have diagonal lines parallel to the material's edges. Depending on whether the material contracts in anisotropic directions as it heats up, this new phase can either be asymmetric or symmetric about the material's center, and these properties can be inferred from fluctuations in the material's magnetism. However, further research is necessary to fully understand these temperature-dependent transitions in the material.

The study presents initial findings on (2+1)-D relativistic viscous hydrodynamics simulations 
of the ALICE Pb-Pb collision data at the LHC, specifically examining thermal photons 
emitted at various polar angles in the transverse plane. By constraining the ratio of lateral 
to longitudinal photon momentum anisotropy ($\hat{a}_T$) and systematic azimuthal angle 
$\Psi_\Pi$, the viscosity-to-entropy ratio ($\eta/s$) is calculated over a range of collision 
centralities. At 20-30% central Pb-Pb collisions, the LHC's conditions, the simulated 
$\eta/s$ values with thermal photons show a small deviation from the flat distribution, 
exhibiting the effects of higher viscosity at lower collision centralities. Furthermore, 
the model shows that low-mass thermal photons have anisotropic emission with a higher 
momentum anisotropy ($\hat{a}_T$) during early and late particle formation times. This indicates 
the properties of early and late formed particles are similar. As a result, by comparing the 
thermal photons' anisotropic behavior to that of charged particles, the study reveals the 
properties of the quark-gluon plasma created in the LHC's conditions, which dominates 
the early stages of the collision process.

On a geometric basis, we investigate non-coplanar spin arrangements with topological stability in triangular and kagome lattices. These configurations are consistent with topological spin-1/2 models such as TlDeFe2(PO4)3 and CoNiNbO4, which have a non-Abelian spin-1/2 character. Furthermore, our analysis sheds light on the potential spin-3/2 ordering in CoNiNbO4. The research also establishes a connection with recently discovered experimental findings, and demonstrates that triangular and kagome structures can host a variety of non-trivial spin arrangements.

We tackle a critical issue in vast testing scenarios where numerous interventions yield inconsistent results, rendering conventional control of false discovery rates (FDR) ineffectual. In response, we develop a protocol to systematically eliminate unconvincing findings before controlling FDR. This novel strategy, called R-FDR, guarantees that the resulting controlled FDR stays low, even in data sets showing strong correlations among tests. Utilizing R-FDR, we successfully decreases the overall number of unnecessary interventions across a range of non-linear network simulation settings. Moreover, through simulations on a massive COVID-19 contact network, we demonstrate that R-FDR substantially amplifies the detection rate of valid interventions, reaching up to 7 times the rate achieved through conventional FDR control methods.

The notion of scale factor evolution is a fundamental aspect of modern cosmology, closely tied to the concept of a uniformly expanding universe. In standard cosmological model, objects at distance $r$ from each other move apart at an accelerating rate, their distances apart increasing as $a(t)$ raises. However, there exists an alternative theory that diverges from this conventional model by replacing the linear scale factor with a non-linear function of BAO distances and time, thereby retaining the benefits of scale factor evolution while adhering to static BAO patterns. To bridge the gap between this alternative theory and the conventional cosmological model, this study seeks to examine various cosmological observables, including Hubble parameters, deceleration parameters, distance moduli, and distance to reinvestigate the relationship between scale factor evolution and cosmological models with a fixed, uniformly expanding universe. In doing so, this investigation aims to identify which such models have the potential to describe the observed static BAO patterns, as well as the distance-luminosity relation of optical and gamma-ray bursts.

The CDF II Collaboration has made a precise measurement of the W boson mass which deviates from the Standard Model's prediction, and when combined with another anomaly in the muon's magnetic moment, it strongly suggests that a beyond-the-standard-model explanation is needed. In this research, we examine the potential of a type-X two Higgs doublet model in resolving both issues simultaneously. Specifically, we concentrate on the type-X two Higgs doublet model with an additional discrete Z2 symmetry, which doublets can only be combined. Our analysis shows that the discrepancy in the W boson's mass can be remedied by adding a light, around 225 GeV, pseudoscalar boson, which also has a positive effect on the discrepancy in the muon's magnetic moment. However, introducing a light pseudoscalar also results in a larger prediction for the gamma ray signal in the direct detection of dark matter, thus limiting this model's potential to resolve this problem. In contrast, our results also show that the type-X 2HDM with a 225 GeV pseudoscalar, but without discrete symmetry, cannot simultaneously resolve the W boson and muon anomalies.

Our proposed system, SWIFTER, instantly modifies search queries to identify previously unknown concepts. It works by using the MeaningRank API to analyze the meanings of a user's search history, and with every new term, the system identifies new concepts and relevant synonyms through on demand crowdsourcing on Amazon Mechanical Turk. These discovered concepts and their associated synonyms are then incorporated into the original search query to provide the user with novel information. In our evaluation, SWIFTER successfully detected 17 previously understood concepts across various real-world demonstrations, and with an expanded search history, the system efficiently processed new terms in under 200 milliseconds.

This paper presents an in-depth examination of a novel unsupervised challenge, aiming to establish a method for quantifying oral dialogue synchronization from speech signals. In the absence of synchronized reference dialogue videos, a deep neural synchronization distance is proposed to gauge conversational speech synchronization. Undersupervised learning is employed to derive a novel synchronization distance that leverages paired utterance pairs and non-paired utterances. A deep neural synchronization distance is developed to measure conversational speech synchronization, comprising a deep neural model trained to recognize synchronized conversational dialogue pairs and a model trained to recognize disparate conversational dialogue pairs. Three deep neural models, including a robust neural model, are explored to measure conversational speech synchronization. Results from two speech synthesis datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed deep neural synchronization distance in distinguishing synthesized speech from human speech.

It has been approximately eight years since the initial release of the open-source 
Python library, RCSED. The platform enables users to generate various plots 
such as 2D, 1D spectra, and maps with a range of depiction options including 
galaxy mainlings, PDR emission, X-ray absorption, and more. The deposition file 
is available under version 2.0 incorporating the following updates. 
Deposition files now incorporate the ability to automatically scale the 
depiction based on the data's maximal and minimal values or to set them manually 
as a direct consequence of RCSED being specifically designed for the analysis 
of astronomical data. Furthermore, the implementation has been augmented with 
the capability to handle both symmetric and asymmetric x and y axes, including 
the ability to set a secondary tick size for the axes. Additionally, the 
implementation has been augmented with an axis magnetique, or 'invisible' tick, 
and the capability to include a grid that is depicted within the plot. 
Deposition files now also incorporate the ability to include a legend which 
enables users to distinguish between different data sets. The deposition file 
is available under version 2.0 incorporating the above updates and may be 
accessed via the URL, https://github.com/astrodude95/RCSEDv2.

Classifying every action occurring at the frame level in every video is a difficult task. Most existing models focus solely on accurate action recognition rather than mapping actions to video frames. As a result, they struggle to recognize dense, dense actions in uncued videos. To overcome this limitation, we establish the first systematic method for directly linking videos to fine-grained action frames. By developing dense action features and joint dense activity mapping, our approach learns rich, dense activity representations without human supervision. Additionally, it accurately maps video frames to action labels without requiring video-level supervision. Our experiments show that our method outperforms other approaches, improving UNSupervised Temporal Action Segmentation by as much as 14% on the ActivityNet v1.3 dataset.

Three sets of hidden-charm pentaquark systems are identified, each having distinct $SU(3)_F$ quantum numbers, and their underlying connections to the decays of $\Xi_{cc}^+$ are explored through two-step processes, with the intermediate states being $\Xi'_{cc}$, $\Sigma_{cc}(2500)$, or $\Omega_{cc}$. Utilizing the treatment of the baryon light-front wave functions by Ding and Liu, the differential angular distributions and total decay rates for these $\Xi_{cc}^+$ decays are determined. The derived results, however, differ from those obtained by the Hangzhou group and the SuSHYFT group, respectively, which may indicate inconsistencies in the Hagedorn density matrix element or the wave functions used by these two groups. The constructed $\Omega_{cc}^{+}(3240)$, further being treated as an interpolating current, yields a mass of approximately 3240 MeV,, which is in line with the LHCb experimental findings. The difficulty in achieving a mass consensus might be, at least partially, attributed to the fact that the density matrix element used by the SuSHYFT group has yet to be implemented.
